newsitem.title: FRANCE: Paris Club reschedules Mozambique debt.
newsitem.headline: Paris Club reschedules Mozambique debt.

text.p: The Paris Club of creditor nations said on Thursday it had agreed to restructure Mozambique's debt and, in a departure from tradition, signalled a willingness to hold further talks if the debt relief was not enough.

It said in a statement it had agreed a two-thirds write-off of payments due in the rescheduling period, under so-called Naples terms of debt relief, the most generous currently available for the world's poorest countries.
The agreement would save Mozambique $660 million in payments due in the three-year period covered by the agreement.

"Creditor countries furthermore declared themselves ready to invite the Republic of Mozambique to a new meeting on the basis of an appropriate arrangement with the IMF (International Monetary Fund), the statement said.

The Paris Club has said it is willing to improve debt relief available to the world's poorest nations on a case-by-case basis, offering a write-off of up to 80 percent of the stock of debt if requested to do so by a debtor country.
In a preliminary list drawn up by the World Bank and the IMF earlier this year, Mozambique was cited as one of the countries facing unsustainable levels of debt.
Such generous terms, agreed in September, can only be obtained after signing an agreement on economic reforms, and have not yet been offered to any country.

The improved terms are part of a joint initiative with the World Bank and IMF which are also looking at ways of lifting the burden of debt owed to them and other mutilateral agencies by poor countries.
A source close to IMF and World Bank discussions on debt relief said countries which may benefit early include Bolivia, Uganda and Guyana. Mozambique is seen as a candidate next year.
The debt relief initiative is designed to help countries which despite efforts to implement economic reforms, see the gains of economic growth eaten up by heavy debt service charges.
Uganda in particular has been cited often by international officials as one with a good record on economic reforms but problematic levels of debt charges.

In Paris on Wednesday, however, World Bank President James Wolfensohn said it was unlikely the first cases in the debt relief plan would be finalised before a meeting of the IMF and World Bank in April.
"They will probably not be concluded, but they will be running," he told Reuters.
Paris Club sources have stressed there is no list of countries which are likely to benefit first from improved debt relief, saying that all countries will be treated on a case-by-case basis.
